cases.answer: I use the same order every time so nothing gets skipped. First, I compare my findings with the previous shift's assessment in the electronic health record and look for anything that changed. Then I recheck any abnormal vital sign myself, with a second set of readings a few minutes later, before I act on it. Finally, before I hand over, I read back the key findings to the patient or their family to make sure I heard their symptoms correctly. This matters because a missed change in breathing or blood pressure can turn into a deterioration that nobody catches until it is serious. Afterwards I document what I found and what I did, and if I notice I missed something, I tell my charge nurse and add it to my personal checklist so it doesn't happen again.

I go through it in a fixed order. First I check the patient's vital signs and compare them with the last set in the chart. Then I do a head-to-toe assessment, listening to the lungs and checking skin, pain and mobility. Finally I ask the patient how they feel compared with yesterday, and I compare that with what I found.
I double check everything and ask a colleague if I'm unsure.

When my grandmother was in hospital after a fall, the nurse on her ward was the one who noticed she was getting confused at night and pushed for her medication to be reviewed. That changed how I saw the job: nurses are the people who watch closely and speak up. I want to do that work. I'm calm under pressure and I'm good at noticing small changes; in my care assistant job I spotted a resident's swollen ankle that turned out to be a blood clot, and I reported it the same hour. As a registered nurse I'd be doing patient assessment, giving medication safely and planning care with the doctors and the family, and those are the parts I'm most drawn to.

I have always wanted to help people and I think nursing is a very rewarding career. I am a hard worker and a people person, and I believe I would be a great fit for any team. Nursing offers good job security and lots of opportunities to grow, which is important to me for my future.

Reason: patient care. Strengths: communication, teamwork, empathy, patient assessment, medication administration, care planning. Example: example. Role: registered nurse, patients, doctors, families. I want to because I care. Specific. Genuine. Strengths connect to the job. I learned a lot. Result: 100%. Situation, task, action, result.

My biggest strength is staying organised when the ward is busy. Last winter I was working nights on a 28-bed medical ward when two admissions arrived at once and we were one nurse short. I was responsible for six patients, including both new ones. I triaged them by how unwell they were, I asked the healthcare assistant to take the routine observations on my stable patients, and I completed both admission assessments within the first hour. Nobody's medication was late that night, and the morning handover started on time. My second strength is communication: I explained the delays to one worried family, and they thanked me afterwards. What I learned is to ask for help early instead of trying to do everything myself.

We are a really strong team on our unit. Last year we had a big rise in falls on the ward, so we got together and we came up with a new plan. We put alarms on the beds of the patients at risk, we did hourly rounding and we changed the handover sheet. We cut falls a lot over the next few months and we were proud of it. I think my strength is that I'm a team player.

On a surgical ward last spring, a patient I was looking after had his operation cancelled for the second time because an emergency took the theatre. He had been fasting since midnight and his daughter had taken the day off work. Before I went in, I checked with the surgical team when the new date was likely to be and what we could offer him, so I would have facts rather than apologies. I sat down with him and his daughter, told them straight away that the operation would not happen today, and explained why. I arranged a meal for him immediately and I booked a call with the surgeon for that afternoon. He was upset at first, but he said he appreciated being told early and honestly, and he was rebooked within 3 days. I learned that people cope better with bad news when they get it early, with a plan attached.

cases.answer: so this was on the cardiac ward last year and i had to tell a patient that his test results meant he could not go home for his daughters wedding that weekend i prepared by reading the results with the doctor first and asking what options we had then i sat with him in a quiet room and told him clearly and kindly what the results meant and i offered to call his daughter with him we arranged a video call from the ward during the ceremony and he watched the whole thing he told me it was the best he could have hoped for i learned that bad news lands better when you bring something you can still do

I'd start by finding out where we actually are. I'd audit twenty sets of recent assessment notes, look at the early warning scores we missed in the last quarter, and ask the nurses on each shift what gets in the way. Then I'd act in three steps: first, agree one assessment standard with the team, using the early warning score and a short head-to-toe checklist; second, run ten-minute huddle sessions at shift change where we practise on real cases; third, pair newer nurses with experienced ones for a month. I'd measure success by the share of patients with a complete assessment documented within an hour of admission, which I'd expect to rise from around 70% to 90% in three months. Throughout, I'd listen to the team's concerns and keep it respectful, because people resist standards that are imposed on them without being heard.

I would gather information first by asking the team what they find hard, and then I'd set clear steps for every assessment. To be honest, though, I wouldn't really ask anyone, I'd just tell them the new rules on day one because asking takes too long. I'd measure success by checking that assessments are complete within an hour of admission, aiming for 90%. I'd make sure we use the early warning score on every patient. I would listen to everyone respectfully, although if they push back I'd just overrule them.

In the first two weeks I'd gather information: read the last three months of patient survey comments, sit in on handovers, and ask patients and the doctors on the ward what frustrates them most. I'd expect noise at night and slow answers to call bells to come up. Then I'd pick the two biggest problems and fix them in order: first, quiet hours from 11 pm with lights dimmed; second, a rule that call bells are answered within five minutes, with the nurse in charge checking a sample every shift. The trade-off is that the time for call-bell checks comes out of other admin, so I'd drop the weekly paperwork audit for those 90 days and explain that decision to the ward manager. I'd talk to the team, the patients and the doctors every fortnight about progress. Success means the satisfaction score rising from 72% to 80% by day 90, with call-bell response time as the early signal.

In my last job as a barista I improved our cafe's customer reviews in three months. First I read every online review and asked regulars what annoyed them. Then I changed the morning rota so two people were on the coffee machine at the busiest hour, and I trained the new staff on milk steaming. Our average rating went from 3.9 to 4.5 stars. I learned that small, visible changes win people back.

If a patient refused part of an assessment, say a blood pressure check at 2 am, I'd first listen to why. Often they're exhausted or worried about what the result means, so I'd keep it respectful and acknowledge that. I'd explain to the patient why the observation matters tonight, for example after a new heart medication, and offer a compromise: one reading now, and the full set at the morning round. The trade-off is less information overnight, which I'd accept only if their early warning score was stable; if it wasn't, I'd explain that the check can't wait and involve the doctor. Afterwards I'd document the refusal and the conversation in the notes, tell the next shift, and check back with the patient in the morning.

I'd stay calm and listen to the patient's concerns without interrupting, and I'd keep my tone respectful even if they were angry. I'd explain what the assessment involves and why I need to do it. If they still said no, I'd respect that and move on to my next patient.

cases.answer: I'd do it in three stages. First, they shadow me for two shifts while I talk through each assessment out loud: airway, breathing, circulation, then the early warning score and what I document in the electronic record. Second, they do the assessments while I watch, and I give them feedback straight after each patient. Third, they work on their own with me checking a sample of their notes for a week. I'd only sign them off once I'd seen them pick up a deteriorating patient correctly in a simulation, because that's the moment that matters. I'd explain why it matters from day one: a missed change in a patient's breathing can turn into a cardiac arrest a few hours later.
Show them how I do it, let them try, then check their notes.

cases.answer: Medication that is time-critical comes first: insulin, antibiotics and pain relief can't be late without harm, so I'd give those on time and do a focused assessment on anyone whose early warning score is rising. The trade-off is that full head-to-toe assessments on stable patients move later in the shift, which I'd accept because a late antibiotic does more damage than a later routine check. I'd tell the nurse in charge straight away that I'm behind, and ask the doctor to review any patient I'm worried about. For example, on a night with three admissions I gave all the 10 pm medications on time, flagged two stable patients for later checks, and caught up by midnight with help from the healthcare assistant.

Trade-off: I would prioritise and decide what matters. Specifics: patient assessment, medication administration, IV pumps, electronic health records. Why it matters: safety matters because patients matter. Communication: I would talk to the right people, patients and doctors. Example: for example, an example from my experience.
